olszewski:asplos:2012: The citing record is small but attentive: most of it comes from the data-race-detection literature, and an unusually large share of those works discuss the system in technical depth rather than in passing. IFRit measures against Aikido as a detector of comparable accuracy; OCTET and Kard, which builds lightweight race detection on per-thread memory protection, position their designs relative to its hypervisor-based approach; and RADISH gives its page-protection technique a detailed reading when arguing for its own mechanisms. Citation is confined to one community, but within it the paper is read as a serious design point for low-overhead sharing detection.
del2018: External reception is slight and mostly taxonomic. Surveys of FPGA programming and of high-level synthesis toolchains include FROST among the systems that carry DSLs to hardware, the stateful dataflow multigraphs work positions its data-centric approach relative to FROST's scheduling co-language, and high-level synthesis compilers such as AnyHLS and FLOWER cite it among prior DSL-to-hardware efforts. Few external works build on the system itself; its main uptake ran through Tiramisu, and elsewhere it stands as one entry in the catalogue of paths from high-level languages to FPGAs.
agarwal:suif:1997: A problem statement rather than a solution, the workshop paper draws a small citing record, much of it unjudged. The engagement that exists is close to home: MIT theses building Raw's software stack — software-based instruction caching, software floating-point computation, the fabric hardware implementation — cite it as a working document of the compiler effort. Farther out, surveys of coarse-grained reconfigurable architectures and of reconfigurable computing systems include it in their accounts of the area. Its reception is that of a project charter, cited chiefly from within the project it chartered.
vemal-neurips: Citing works engage Vemal almost entirely from a distance: none extends the method or deploys the learned policy, and the record is peripheral throughout. The paper appears as an example — one of the demonstrations that learned policies can stand in for hand-written compiler heuristics — in a survey of machine learning for computer architecture and systems, in a taxonomy of ML for systems problems, and in the related-work sections of learned-optimization efforts such as ProGraML, RL4ReAl, and work on vectorization heuristics in dynamic compilers. The literature records it as a data point in a trend rather than a foundation.
chen:pldi:2022: The citation record is mostly brief: auto-vectorization papers list the framework among SLP extensions when surveying the landscape, and systems such as Parsimony and DynVec cite it as an example of the genre. The engaged citations are positional — work on hybrid slice selection for SLP, on retrofitting control-flow graphs in LLVM IR for auto-vectorization, and the compiler-construction paper If-Convert as Early as You Must each set their designs against its predicate-based approach. The paper has entered the frame of reference for control-flow vectorization; whether Predicated SSA itself is taken up is a question the early record does not answer. Evaluated artifacts accompany the paper at the Zenodo archive.
zhao:pact:2006: The record around it is small, and its center of gravity moved toward security analysis: TaintPipe adopted the idea of a compact recorded profile driving a later analysis for pipelined symbolic taint tracking, and StraightTaint extended it into decoupled offline taint analysis, putting the profile to uses the original paper did not anticipate. PiPA likewise built directly on the work. Elsewhere the engagement is documentary: tracing and debugging systems such as ONTRAC and work on hierarchical program paths discuss the profile's design, and PROMPT measures its own memory-profiling framework against it. The citations are few, but a good share come from people building comparable machinery.
chen:graphics-hardware:2005: A small citation record splits between two communities. In graphics architecture, a power-aware reconfigurable rendering engine adopted the idea of reallocating pipeline resources, work on dynamic reconfigurable shaders for embedded graphics positions itself against the compile-time approach, and GRAMPS and later work on fine-grain scheduling of pipeline parallelism cite the paper as an example of mapping the graphics pipeline onto programmable parallel hardware. In the streaming community, its rendering workloads reappear as benchmarks for mapping stream programs to multicore processors. Most mentions are brief, and the paper reads in the literature as a data point on reconfigurable rendering rather than a foundation later systems built on.
del2017common: Beyond that follow-on, the external record is slender and mostly taxonomic. Surveys of FPGA programming abstractions and of high-level synthesis tools and toolchains place FROST among DSL-to-FPGA backends, and papers such as iPIM and work on transformations of high-level synthesis codes cite it as one instance of the DSL-to-HLS route. A few applied efforts in hardware-accelerated image and signal processing cite its speedups as evidence that FPGA acceleration pays. There is little building on the system outside its authors' orbit; in the literature the paper stands as a catalogued point in the design space of FPGA toolchains. The compiler lives on in the Tiramisu-Compiler/tiramisu repository.
g2-cgo21: The external record is compact and split between comparison and cataloguing. Work on decoupling schedule, topology layout, and algorithm in GPU graph processing takes G2 as a baseline, an FPGA high-level-synthesis study of graph analysis measures against it, and Voyager builds on it for graph neural networks; a survey of optimization techniques for GPU programming in ACM Computing Surveys covers its scheduling space. Most other citations list G2 among GPU graph frameworks — A Programming Model for GPU Load Balancing and several accelerator papers cite it in that role — a modest but substantive reception for a system whose ideas also travel through its successors. The compiler lives on in the GraphIt-DSL/graphit repository.
sheldon:lcpc:2001: The external record is thin, and much of it unjudged, but the audience it found is a particular one: hardware synthesis. Devos's work on loop transformations for the optimized generation of reconfigurable hardware builds directly on the techniques, and the optimizations are cited in FPGA design methodology using streaming, in expression synthesis for process networks generated by LAURA, and in constructing application-specific memory hierarchies on FPGAs — settings where array transformations introduce exactly the divisions and modulos the paper eliminates. A later treatment of modulo-based array indexing in loops positions itself against the approach, evidence that the problem, if narrow, kept its relevance.
zhao:cgo:2007: Citation of UMI is sparse and mostly brief. The works that engage it sit in the online-profiling literature: RapidMRC and PiPA cite its results as evidence about the costs and feasibility of profiling memory behavior at runtime, and papers on cache-utility measurement and on automatic prefetching by binary rewriting position their designs against it. The rest is passing mention among lightweight profiling techniques, in work spanning full-system memory tracing, adaptive prefetching, and shared-cache management. The methodology registered in its community without, in the judged record, being adopted as a running system.
zhao:wbia:2005: The citation record is thin and consists mostly of list membership: works on memory allocators, mobile systems, and data-center software cite the paper as one instance of dynamic memory optimization, typically in a sentence. The closer engagements are scattered. MMT, exploiting fine-grained parallelism in dynamic memory management, reuses its experimental setting, as does symbolic range analysis of pointers; Cling, a memory allocator to mitigate dangling pointers, discusses its context-based pooling in some detail. The paper circulates mainly as a named example of runtime pool allocation and prefetching rather than as a base that later systems build on.
asplos013: The citing literature is small but comes from the community the work targets. Distributed stream-processing systems treat Gloss as a design point to differentiate from: Megaphone and Meces, both concerned with reconfiguring running dataflows, position their state-migration designs against it. The self-adaptation line of Vogel, Griebler, and colleagues cites its results as evidence, in a systematic review of self-adaptation for parallel stream processing and in work on transparent adaptation of stream parallel patterns. The remaining citations are passing mentions in papers on rescaling and elasticity — a modest record, concentrated where live reconfiguration is actually studied.
pacula:evoapps:2012: The record beyond the project is thin and almost entirely peripheral, and part of its influence runs through the SiblingRivalry autotuner it served rather than the paper itself. Surveys carry most of what there is: Wang and O'Boyle's surveys of machine learning in compiler optimization list the study among autotuning applications, and a survey of adaptive operator selection for meta-heuristics places it in that lineage. Online-learning papers on bandits and perturbation techniques cite it as an applied example, Tensor Comprehensions names it in passing among autotuning precedents, and HybridTuner discusses the hyperparameter question in some detail. Cited by surveyors more than builders, the reception matches its role as a focused companion study. The underlying PetaBricks system lives on in the petabricks/petabricks repository.
zhao:ismm:2010: External reception is sparser and concentrated in the shadow-memory niche. AddressSanitizer differentiates its shadow mapping from EMS64's displacement scheme, and the PROMPT memory-profiling framework measures against it as a baseline; Skadu cites its results as evidence in its treatment of vector shadow memories, and papers on page overlays and Java metadata tracking list it among shadow-memory designs. The remaining citations are passing mentions. This is a technique cited by the small community that builds shadow-memory systems, mostly to situate their own mappings.
tiramisu-auto: Outside that direct line, external engagement is small and mostly glancing. The model appears in related-work sections of the tensor-program autotuning literature — TLP differentiates its cost model from it, and systems from PolyGym to multi-pass autotuning frameworks list it among learned cost models — but few external works engage its mechanics. The clearest continuation is the work on supporting dynamic program sizes in deep-learning cost models, which extends the model itself. The paper is cited, in short, as one instance of a broader direction: learned cost models inside compiler search.
bruening:fddo:2000: Softspec's citation record is largely unjudged, and the judged portion is small. What that portion shows is a place in the thread-level speculation literature: the TOPLAS survey of compiler-driven software speculation covers it, work on a speculative mechanism for barrier synchronization adopts its idea, and studies of thread-level speculation for web applications and JavaScript engines cite it when motivating speculation without hardware support, while master/slave speculative parallelization positions itself against it. When the paper is cited substantively, it is as a demonstration that speculative parallelism needs no special hardware.
chou-pldi20-taco-conversion: Within the sparse-compilation literature the work registers as part of taco's format story. Successor sparse compilers position themselves relative to it: SparseTIR and UniSparse treat the generated conversion routines as a point of departure or a baseline for format customization, and the MLIR sparse-tensor compiler discusses the approach in detail. The work on compiling modular and general sparse workspaces builds on the machinery directly, and papers across sparse linear algebra — from Gamma's sparse matrix multiplication to AlphaSparse's generated SpMV codes — cite the conversion measurements as evidence that format choice and conversion cost matter. The remaining citations are brief mentions in the tensor-compiler literature. The implementation lives on in the tensor-compiler/taco repository, and an evaluated artifact accompanies the paper.
larsen:micro:2005: Citations from elsewhere are few and mostly brief: the paper appears in related-work lists on SIMD code generation — dynamic-programming selection of vector instructions, Liquid SIMD, data-layout transformation for stencils — typically in a sentence noting that vectorization can be applied selectively. A handful go further. Hampton and Asanović built on the compiler in implementing virtual memory in a vector processor with software restart markers, a dissertation on SIMD-aware word-length optimization adopted its approach, and work mapping streaming languages to general-purpose processors through vectorization discusses the algorithm in detail. The reception is confined to the short-vector compilation community, and modest even there.
barua:hpc:1998: Much of the citation mass lies within the project itself, in the Maps, RAWCC, and silicon-compilation line that absorbed the transformation, and the external record is correspondingly thin. Where outside work engages it, it does so substantively: DEFACTO positions its bridge between compilation and synthesis against the bank-disambiguation approach, and work on high-level compilation for gate-reconfigurable architectures and on datapath and memory co-optimization for FPGA-based computation discusses the technique in detail. A few compiler papers, among them work on cache-penalty optimizations for the Itanium 2 processor, cite it in passing — a modest record, read mainly by compiler writers targeting partitioned memories.
kotkar:hci4cid:2008: Its citation record is slight and consists of passing mentions. The citing works come from the literature on voice interfaces for development — the spoken web application framework, spoken query systems for agricultural commodity prices, community-driven maps for developing regions, and studies of interactive voice response as a participatory medium — each naming the Audio Wiki in a sentence among prior voice-based systems for low-literacy users. Most of the external citations are unjudged, and none of the judged ones engages the design, so the paper survives in that literature as one entry in the roll call of early spoken-web proposals.
buildit-cgo21: External reception is thinner than the project's own lineage: outside the group, BuildIt appears mostly as an entry in the multi-stage-programming canon. Papers from that community — on partially evaluating symbolic interpreters, on multi-stage evaluators with let-insertion, and on mechanized semantics of staging annotations — cite it as the C++ point in the design space, and SABLE lists it among staging frameworks for sparse computation. eCC++ positions its embedded-DSL framework against it directly, while systems such as SLANG.D, Flan, and Exo 2 mention it in passing as related infrastructure. The citations are few but come from the community the paper addresses. The framework lives on in the BuildIt-lang/buildit repository.
agrawal:cases:2005: Outside the project the record is thin and mostly brief: stream-architecture and stream-compiler papers — software-pipelined execution on GPUs, Liquid Metal, the Fei Teng 64 stream processing system — name the analysis among StreamIt's optimizations rather than build on it. The more substantive engagements treat it as a neighbor to be distinguished from: Sigma* positions its own work against this compile-time framework, and the paper on fusing effectful comprehensions describes the approach closely. A record of this size and shape says the framework was noted more than adopted — its generality acknowledged, its machinery left to the project that built it. The StreamIt compiler infrastructure, including this analysis, lives on in the bthies/streamit repository.
shajii:oopsla:2019: The citing record is small but leans toward use: bioinformatics systems adopted Seq as working infrastructure, from segmental-duplication analysis of genome assemblies to the Sequre framework for secure multiparty computation over biomedical data and its successor Shechi. Some of that engagement reaches the language through the Codon compiler it grew into, and the remainder of the citations name Seq among high-performance languages for the domain rather than engaging its design. An archival artifact accompanies the paper.
looplets-cgo23: External engagement stays close to home. The citation record is small and concentrated in the sparse- and structured-array-compilation community: Galley builds its query optimizer for sparse tensor programs over the abstraction, the compilation of shape operators on sparse arrays and work on load-balanced partitioning of unstructured sparse tensor algebra use it, a mechanized algebra of verified data structures adopts its approach to structure, and work on compressing structured tensor algebra defines itself against it. Beyond that circle the paper appears in a chronology of scheduling languages and in compiler lists. The audience is narrow, but the works at its center engage the language itself. The implementation lives in willow-ahrens/Finch.jl, and a reusable artifact with reproduced results accompanies the paper.
